title: Inventory and Language
premise: Zephyrine Blackwood, a professional translator in her forties, is losing Vessic, the invented childhood language she and her late mother spoke to keep their secrets safe from her father. When renovating her mother's house, she finds a box of forty undelivered letters—her mother's, addressed to a woman named Odile in Marseille—that reveal a hidden love and a deliberate erasure. As Zephyrine translates them, she realizes her mother chose silence over love and passed that silence down like an inheritance; meanwhile Zephyrine's own marriage is quietly dissolving under the same habit of unsaid things. The novel ends with Zephyrine traveling to Marseille to deliver the final letter to a dying Odile, speaking aloud—in broken Vessic—the goodbye her mother never managed, and returning home to say the truest sentence of her own life before it is too late.
about_author: Rosalind Joubert is a former lexicographer who spent a decade cataloguing endangered dialects before turning to fiction. She writes from a narrow house in Brittany, where she keeps, by her own count, 312 unfinished letters.

chapters.title: The Weight of Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. A translator at a conference mistranslates a single word and realizes Vessic, her secret childhood language with her mother, is slipping from her memory word by word. She begins a notebook inventory of everything she can no longer say. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as professional embarrassment.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Clearing her dead mother's house for sale, she pries loose a panel behind the wardrobe and finds a shoebox: forty letters, sealed, stamped, never sent, all addressed to one name—Odile. She recognizes her mother's handwriting but not her mother. Emotional beat: vertigo, the ground of family history tilting.

chapters.title: What the Father Kept
chapters.summary: Alternating with brief flashbacks to young Zephyrine. Her father, rigid and grieving in his own way, visits the house and nearly discovers the box; Zephyrine hides it inside a translation manuscript. We learn how silence was the household's native tongue. Emotional beat: claustrophobic loyalty to old lies.

chapters.title: Odile
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She deciphers the first letters: her mother spent a summer in Marseille at twenty-two and loved a woman there, then chose her father, respectability, and erasure—and taught her daughter a private language built from what couldn't be spoken. Emotional beat: grief braided with a strange new intimacy with the dead.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She catalogs the letters like a professional, numbering and dating them, and notices her own marriage mirrors the archive: her husband Theo has stopped asking questions years ago. A dinner scene where three important sentences go unsaid. Emotional beat: recognition of inherited patterns.

chapters.title: The Unsent Reply
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, first time shifting perspective. He finds Zephyrine translating at 3 a.m., weeping without sound, and understands he has been living beside a locked room for fifteen years. He writes a letter of his own and doesn't send it either. Emotional beat: tender, devastating parallelism.

chapters.title: Marseille, Secondhand
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Through the middle letters she reconstructs her mother's lost summer: the sea, Odile's laugh rendered in Vessic because no French word was sufficient. Her father calls demanding she hurry the house sale. She lies to him fluently. Emotional beat: rising defiance.

chapters.title: The Last Letter Is Blank
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. The final letter contains only her mother's salutation and nothing else—a goodbye never composed. That night Zephyrine's own health scare (a fainting spell, hospital tests) makes mortality concrete: time is running out for her goodbyes too. Emotional beat: fear sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Climax. Zephyrine confronts her father with the letters; he confesses he always knew and begged her mother to stay, and his rigidity cracks into raw, ugly, human grief. Then she boards the train south, leaving Theo a letter that finally says everything. Emotional beat: rupture and release.

chapters.title: Delivered
chapters.summary: Resolution. In a hospice in Marseille, Zephyrine reads all forty letters to the dying Odile, then speaks the missing goodbye in halting, half-remembered Vessic—out loud, properly, at last. Returning home, she says the truest sentence of her life to Theo, whether or not it saves the marriage. Emotional beat: hard-won peace; language recovered by spending it.
